name: LockedUSB Charge Only Adapter
price_note: Listed price at Hacker Warehouse; item shown out of stock at time of check.
skill_note: Plug in between a cable and a charger/port. No configuration of any kind.
build_note: Fixed-function molded adapter, nothing to assemble or flash.
summary: A small USB-A male-to-female pass-through adapter that physically omits or disconnects the D+/D- data pins so a phone or laptop plugged in through it can only draw power, not exchange data. It is a defensive accessory for using untrusted public USB charging ports (airports, hotels, conference kiosks), not an attack tool.
honest_take: It does exactly one boring thing and does it fine, but it solves a narrower problem than people think: it protects you from a malicious wall socket or charging kiosk reading your device over the data pins ('juice jacking'), not from a malicious cable. If the cable itself is the implant - like an O.MG Cable - the compromise already happened at the cable, upstream of where this adapter sits, and the blocker does nothing. There's also no chip disclosed, so 'DCP charging mode support' just means it fakes the resistor/voltage handshake phones expect on a dumb charger; some phones will still only trickle-charge through it.
best_for: Charging a phone from an unknown public USB port or kiosk
Handing to non-technical people as a cheap, foolproof precaution
not_for: Protecting against a malicious cable (the threat has to be in the wall/port, not the cable)
Fast charging on some phones that require data-pin negotiation for higher wattage

hardware.mcu_primary_note: No MCU disclosed. Vendor copy describes a charge-detect front end (DCP mode signalling, output short-circuit 'hiccup' protection, ~2.3A limit) implemented with analog/small ASIC parts, not a programmable chip.
hardware.charging: USB-A pass-through (device draws power from whatever port it's plugged into)
notable_physical: USB-A male to USB-A female in-line adapter, no cable

usb_hid_inject.note: No MCU at all; cannot inject keystrokes. Contrast with the O.MG UnBlocker (tracked separately), a wireless implant disguised in this exact form factor.

usb_mass_storage.note: Passes power only; no data path exists to present storage.

usb_ethernet_attack.note: No data pins connected through at all.

usb_keylogger.note: No logic to log anything; purely passive.

usb_exfil.note: This is precisely the attack surface the device exists to block.

usb_payload_lang.note: Not reprogrammable; fixed analog/charge-detect circuit only.

scriptable.note: Fixed-function hardware, nothing to flash or script.

web_ui.note: No connectivity beyond the pass-through power path.

cloud_c2.note: No radio or network stack of any kind.

standalone_untethered.note: Purely a passive inline accessory; it has no autonomous function to run.

legal.notes: Fully legal to own and use everywhere; it is a passive protective accessory with no offensive function.

name: Vidar ATtiny85-based BadUSB
firmware_note: Ships pre-loaded with a demo payload that opens a Windows command prompt and launches a browser to the setup page. User-editable via the Arduino IDE / Digispark-style ATtiny85 toolchain; ships with no on-device way to store or switch between multiple payloads.
price_note: $20 single unit, $15/unit at 3+. Seller listed as 'on break' at time of check - not currently orderable.
skill_note: Plug-and-run for the stock demo payload; editing the payload requires installing the Arduino IDE and an ATtiny85/Digispark board profile.
build_note: Sold pre-built. Ships programmed; no soldering to use it, only to reflash a new payload over USB (Micronucleus-style bootloader, typical of ATtiny85 boards of this kind).
summary: A minimal, very small ATtiny85-based BadUSB stick that enumerates as a USB keyboard and fires a pre-programmed keystroke payload on plug-in. Functionally the same class of device as a Digispark BadUSB or the low end of the Evil Crow Cable line, built by a different one-person hardware shop (rot13labs, Gainesville FL).
honest_take: This is a Digispark-class ATtiny85 keystroke injector in tiny packaging, nothing more. The ATtiny85 has no native USB peripheral, so it almost certainly relies on V-USB (bit-banged software USB), which caps HID reliability and speed well below a real USB-HID microcontroller like the ATmega32U4 in a Rubber Ducky. There's no storage for multiple payloads and no way to trigger a different script without physically re-flashing it from a computer - you get exactly one script running until you reprogram it. At $20 for a fixed single-payload stick, it is priced like a novelty, not a tool; a $5 Digispark clone running the same class of open-source ATtiny85 BadUSB sketch does the identical job.
best_for: One-off, pre-set keystroke-injection demos
Learning how V-USB/ATtiny85 HID BadUSB sticks work
not_for: Field engagements needing multiple switchable payloads
Fast or complex HID injection (V-USB timing is a real bottleneck)

hardware.mcu_primary_note: 8-bit AVR, no native USB peripheral - USB HID is almost certainly implemented in software via the V-USB library, as on Digispark boards of the same class. Not independently confirmed by a public schematic.
hardware.storage: None - payload is compiled into the flashed firmware image
hardware.case: Bare PCB, described by the maker as 'as small as my PCB builder could make'

usb_keylogger.note: Injects keystrokes, does not capture them.

name: Evil Crow Cable
firmware_note: Fixed keystroke-injection firmware for the ATtiny85; scripts are uploaded and reflashed from a host over USB, no on-cable script storage or remote control.
vendor: AprilBrother (manufacturing/PCB); design by Joel Serna and Ernesto Sanchez
price_note: Listed out of stock since 2025-12-06 at time of check.
skill_note: Simple keystroke-injection cable; editing the payload needs the Arduino ATtiny85 toolchain.
build_note: Sold pre-built as a working cable; payload changes are uploaded over USB in seconds per user reports.
summary: The base model in AprilBrother's Evil Crow Cable line: an ATtiny85-based BadUSB built into a working USB cable, with the data lines enabled and no wireless hardware. It is the entry-level, fixed-payload sibling of the ESP32-S3/Wi-Fi-equipped Evil Crow Cable Wind, which is already in this database as a separate, more capable product.
honest_take: Checked against Evil Crow Cable Wind (already tracked here): this is genuinely different hardware, not a rebrand - Wind runs an ESP32-S3 or similar with Wi-Fi and a web control panel for remote-triggered, in-field payload swapping; this base Cable is a plain ATtiny85 with no wireless and no on-device script storage, at roughly half Wind's price. That's a fair trade if you only need to drop one fixed payload and retrieve the cable later, but if you need to change the payload or trigger it without physically pulling the cable, you need Wind (or something like it), not this.
best_for: One-shot, fixed-payload cable drops where you'll retrieve the cable
Cheapest working example of a cable-form BadUSB
not_for: Remote/wireless payload triggering (no radio at all)
Multiple payloads without reflashing

name: EvilDuck SD
firmware_note: Rubber Ducky-style scripting engine (STRING/DELAY/keypress commands) that reads script.txt off a microSD card and executes it as keyboard input on power-up. First-generation hardware in the EvilDuck line, superseded by EvilDuck S3.
vendor: cifertech (open source; no assembled unit sold)
price_note: Estimated bill of materials only: an Arduino Micro (ATmega32U4) clone board plus a microSD breakout, no assembled unit is sold.
skill_note: Requires wiring an SD breakout to specific Arduino Micro pins and flashing the sketch yourself; no vendor-assembled option.
build_note: Arduino Micro + SD card module wired point-to-point (CS/MOSI/MISO/SCK plus a status LED); no PCB sold, breadboard or perfboard build.
summary: The original EvilDuck: an Arduino Micro (ATmega32U4) running a Rubber Ducky-style script interpreter that reads a script.txt file off a microSD card and types it as a real, hardware-native USB keyboard on plug-in, with hot-swap detection for changing the SD card between drops. Open source, DIY-only, no vendor sells an assembled unit.
honest_take: Because the ATmega32U4 has real USB hardware (unlike the ATtiny85 sticks/cables in this same batch), this one gets a genuinely native, low-latency USB HID stack rather than a bit-banged V-USB implementation - a real technical edge over cheaper ATtiny85 BadUSB devices, and functionally very close to the original USB Rubber Ducky's approach (SD card holds the script, no wireless). The catch is it is DIY-only: there's no case, no vendor support, and you're sourcing and wiring an Arduino Micro clone and SD breakout yourself. If you want this exact capability pre-built, pico-ducky and the original Rubber Ducky (both already tracked here) get you there without a soldering iron.
best_for: Learning how SD-card-scripted BadUSB devices work end to end
Cheap, native-USB keystroke injection without buying a commercial Ducky
not_for: Buyers wanting a pre-built, no-solder device
Wireless or remote payload control (see EvilDuck S3 for that)

name: EvilDuck S3
firmware_note: Full DuckScript-style interpreter running on ESP32-S3, adds a browser-based web control panel for uploading, storing and remotely triggering payloads, and autorun-on-plug-in. Second/current generation, replacing the Arduino Micro-based EvilDuck SD.
vendor: cifertech (open source; no assembled unit sold)
price_note: Estimated bill of materials: a generic ESP32-S3 USB dev board (~$6-10) plus passives; no assembled unit sold.
skill_note: Flash-only if using a stock ESP32-S3 dev board; some builds add a WS2812 LED and voltage regulator that need soldering.
build_note: Runs on a generic ESP32-S3 USB dev board; flash the EvilDuck S3 firmware and use the web UI, no custom PCB required for the basic build.
summary: The current-generation EvilDuck: an ESP32-S3 doing both native USB HID and Wi-Fi on one chip, with a browser-based control panel for uploading, storing, and remotely triggering DuckyScript-style payloads. Same open-source project as EvilDuck SD, but a different board and a materially different feature set (wireless, multi-payload, remote trigger vs SD-only, single active script).
honest_take: This is 'ESP32-S3 doing the real work' in the same vein as WiFi Duck and the ESP32-S3 side of Evil Crow Cable Wind - a single cheap SoC handling both HID and Wi-Fi, with a web UI on top. If you already own any ESP32-S3 dev board, the marginal cost of this capability is just flashing new firmware; the value here is entirely the open-source software (payload storage, remote trigger, autorun) rather than unique hardware. Compare directly against commercial devices like the O.MG Cable or Evil Crow Cable Wind before buying dedicated hardware for this - the silicon doing the work is the same class of chip.

Learning how ESP32-S3 HID+WiFi BadUSB firmware is built
not_for: Buyers wanting a finished, cased product with support
Covert form factors - stock ESP32-S3 dev boards look nothing like a normal accessory

name: USBvalve
firmware_note: Version 1.0.0 was a full rewrite onto the Pi Pico SDK (from Arduino IDE) and removed BOOTSEL-button polling to make BadUSB detection more reliable, at the cost of needing a soldered reset button or serial commands to reset. From v0.8.0 it added USB host-mode sniffing to catch HID-injection devices, not just mass-storage access.
vendor: cecio (open source; no assembled unit sold)
price_note: Estimated BOM: a Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040) plus a small I2C OLED, no vendor sells a finished unit.
skill_note: Flashing the pre-built .uf2 is trivial (drag-and-drop bootloader); building the hardware (Pico + OLED, optional custom PCB or 3D-printed spacer) takes basic soldering or careful breadboarding.
build_note: Official pre-built firmware ships as .uf2 for drag-and-drop flashing; hardware assembly (Pico + SSD1306 OLED, optional custom PCB/3D-printed spacer) needs light soldering, though a breadboard build needs none.
summary: A Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040) inline USB inspection tool: in device mode it presents a fake filesystem and shows on an OLED whether a connected host is reading or writing files (catching mass-storage-based exfiltration or drops); from v0.8.0 it can also run in USB host mode to detect a plugged-in device behaving like a keyboard (catching HID-injection BadUSB before you trust it). It is the defensive counterpart to the various BadUSB sticks and cables tracked elsewhere in this database.
honest_take: USBvalve only sees what happens on the USB link it's actually sitting on - it flags file reads/writes to its fake filesystem, or a newly-plugged device announcing itself as a keyboard, and nothing else. It offers no protection against a device that behaves normally at the USB protocol level but is malicious in its payload (e.g., a legitimate-looking flash drive with a booby-trapped file you open yourself), and it has no shielding, so it is explicitly not a tool for safely testing USB Killer-style devices. It's a genuinely well-regarded open-source project (1.3k GitHub stars) with an unusually direct answer to 'is this random USB stick doing something to my computer right now,' which most of the flashier commercial BadUSB-detector gadgets don't actually provide as clearly.
best_for: Sanity-checking an unknown USB drive or cable before trusting it
Teaching how mass-storage exfiltration and HID-injection BadUSB attacks actually look at the USB protocol level
not_for: USB Killer / voltage-attack testing (no isolation or protection circuitry)
Detecting malicious file content on an otherwise well-behaved drive

hardware.battery_note: A community fork (TryBreakFixAgain/USBvalve-tbfa-Mod) adds a LiPo and SD logger; not part of the base project.

name: Multifunction Network Box
firmware_note: Vendor states it 'can run linux and be configured to suit various needs'; no distro, kernel, or software stack disclosed.
vendor: Hacker Warehouse (custom build; underlying hardware OEM not disclosed)
price_note: Model 100 (dual-core Atom 1.6GHz, 2GB RAM, 8x GbE standard/8 max) is $1,500. Model 1000 (Core i5 2.8GHz, 16GB RAM, 8x GbE standard/16 max) is $3,000. Both share the 80GB SSD spec. Custom build, 4-7 week lead time.
skill_note: It's a bare Linux appliance you configure yourself for traffic logging and selective blocking during an engagement; there's no turnkey point-and-click workflow documented.
build_note: Ships as a finished custom-built appliance; a 4-7 week lead time implies it is built to order rather than stocked.
summary: A custom-built, LCD-equipped Linux network appliance with 8-16 Gigabit Ethernet ports, sold by Hacker Warehouse as an all-in-one alternative to running a separate network tap plus a separate logging/blocking host during an engagement. It is positioned as combining traffic logging with active selective blocking, which a passive tap alone cannot do.
honest_take: Strip away the case and LCD and the two tiers are, respectively, a dual-core Atom mini-PC with 2GB of RAM and a Core i5 box with 16GB - ordinary small-form-factor PC hardware with several Ethernet ports, running unspecified Linux software, for $1,500 and $3,000. There is no published detail on the actual blocking mechanism (iptables-style rules? a real inline proxy?), whether the box fails open or closed if it crashes or loses power, or whether it can defeat or merely sits behind things like 802.1X - none of that is documented anywhere in the listing. You are paying almost entirely for Hacker Warehouse's integration and the 'one box for a multi-person engagement' framing; a comparably specced mini-PC with a few USB/PCIe NIC cards and open-source bridging + tcpdump/nftables software would cost a small fraction of this if you're willing to build and validate the software stack yourself.
best_for: Teams that want one physical box handling both logging and selective traffic blocking on an engagement without assembling their own
not_for: Budget-conscious buyers - the premium here is integration, not exotic hardware
Anyone needing documented fail-open/fail-closed behavior for a production network

summary: PiKVM V4 Plus is a legitimate, well-regarded open-source KVM-over-IP appliance built around a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4: it captures a target machine's video (up to 1080p60), emulates a USB keyboard/mouse and a virtual mass-storage drive for OS reinstalls, and controls ATX power - giving BIOS-level remote access over Ethernet, Wi-Fi, or an optional cellular modem card. lab401 resells this exact hardware with 'undetectable hardware RAT for red-team engagements' marketing that is entirely the reseller's framing, not the PiKVM project's.
honest_take: PiKVM is genuinely good, actively maintained open-source engineering, used widely by homelabbers and datacenter admins for exactly what it says: remote BIOS-level access to a machine you own or administer. The 'undetectable' framing is 100% lab401's marketing copy - the official PiKVM site describes it purely as sysadmin/datacenter equipment and never mentions covert or red-team use. What the marketing also glosses over: this is not a drop-in-five-seconds implant like a cable-swap device - you need physical access to plug in HDMI, USB, and power on the target machine, which is a much bigger physical-access requirement than something like an O.MG Cable or Screen Crab. The optional cellular modem (sold as a separate mPCIe card, not built in) does let an operator reach the unit over an out-of-band channel that bypasses the target network's own monitoring, which is the one part of the pitch that's technically accurate.

Red-team engagements with a signed physical-access scope, where an out-of-band cellular channel is explicitly wanted
not_for: Fast, low-physical-access-requirement drops (needs HDMI+USB+power wired in)
Anyone expecting the LTE modem to come installed - it's a separate mPCIe card purchase

name: Dualcomm ETAP-2003 Gigabit Ethernet Tap
price_note: Hacker Warehouse listing (their SKU labeled DC-2003); Dualcomm's own current line names this model family ETAP-2003/ETAP-2003R as the successor to the discontinued DCGS-2005.
skill_note: Plug-and-use hardware, but interpreting captured traffic needs a separate analyzer on the monitor port and real 802.11/Ethernet knowledge.
build_note: Fixed-function hardware tap in a metal case, USB-powered.
summary: A single inline-port, USB-powered 10/100/1000BASE-T copper Ethernet tap with PoE pass-through, in a small metal case. It presents a mirrored copy of both directions of traffic on a monitor port for an external analyzer; unlike the 5-port switch-based tap in this same batch, it is built specifically as a dedicated tap rather than a repurposed switch.
honest_take: Reseller copy for this device family claims 'no power needed' and 'lossless' Gigabit monitoring, but that claim needs scrutiny: full-duplex 1000BASE-T uses all four copper pairs bidirectionally, so a Gigabit tap generally cannot just electrically split the line onto a passive monitor port the way a true zero-power 10/100 tap (like the Throwing Star LAN Tap, already tracked here) can - most designs in this class need active circuitry to aggregate both directions onto a single monitor port, and that circuitry needs power even if the inline link itself might keep passing traffic unpowered. Dualcomm's own site doesn't spell out which parts of this device are truly passive versus USB-powered, so treat any 'can't be detected, no power needed' claim as something to verify yourself with a bench test, not something to take on faith.
best_for: Gigabit-speed passive monitoring where the 10/100-only taps already in this database aren't fast enough
not_for: Assuming zero-power, guaranteed-invisible operation without testing it yourself
Standalone capture - always needs a separate analyzer on the monitor port

name: 10/100 FastE Switch Tap
price_note: Hacker Warehouse listing, Dualcomm model DC-1005PT.
skill_note: Plug in the network path through ports 1-4 and connect an analyzer to the mirrored port 5.
build_note: Fixed-function 5-port switch with mirroring; no assembly needed.
summary: A USB/5VDC-powered 5-port 10/100 Ethernet switch (Dualcomm DC-1005PT) with port-mirroring from Port 1 to Port 5, marketed as a network tap. It is mechanically a real active switch with switching/mirroring logic, not an electrically passive splitter like the Gigabit tap and other true taps in this database.
honest_take: Despite the 'tap' name, this is an ordinary 5-port unmanaged Ethernet switch with SPAN-style port mirroring - genuinely different from a real passive tap, and worse for covert or high-integrity monitoring in two specific ways: a switch's mirror port can silently drop frames under load the way a true passive tap never does, and being a full switch it fails closed (the link goes down, not through) if it loses power, since there is no physical bypass path. At $130 it also sits close to a genuinely passive Gigabit tap's price ($210, also in this database) while offering weaker guarantees. Worth it only if you specifically want several simultaneous 10/100 drops off one mirrored segment; not a stealthier or more reliable alternative to a real passive tap.
best_for: Multiple analysts tapping the same 10/100 segment simultaneously
not_for: High-integrity capture where dropped mirrored frames matter
Fail-open/covert deployments - it goes down, not through, on power loss

It's included here because it's a real hardware security product with independently verifiable specs, but if you're shopping this database for pentest gear, skip it - it belongs next to a home router or a parental-control app, not next to a Wi-Fi Pineapple. At $109 for a ~100Mbps-capable box (per the specs on this specific SKU), it's also well behind Firewalla's current Gigabit-capable models (Blue/Purple/Gold) in raw throughput, which matters directly for whether it can actually inspect traffic on a modern home internet connection without becoming the bottleneck.

name: LittlePcap Network Tap
firmware_note: Firmware is vendor-provided and pre-programmed onto the board's eMMC/SD; no public source repository found. Version 2 documentation points to the underlying NanoPi R3S single-board-computer platform, not a project-specific repo.

build_note: Fixed-function board in a small case, ships ready to use.
summary: An inline dual-Gigabit-Ethernet capture appliance that writes traffic straight to PCAP files on an attached USB drive, with no host computer needed and no IP address of its own on the monitored network. USB-C powered (5V/2A), roughly 16-second boot, and rated to pass a full 1Gbps of traffic - unlike the 10/100-limited passive taps in this database, it is built on an actual small ARM Linux board (NanoPi R3S in v2) rather than a passive electrical splitter.
honest_take: The 'invisible network tap - no IP address' claim is about being unaddressable at layer 3, not about being electrically passive - this is a small ARM Linux single-board computer bridging two Ethernet ports and copying frames to a local file, and it says so itself: no automatic bypass, network connectivity only exists while it's powered on. That means an unplanned reboot or power loss on this box takes the monitored link down with it - something a true zero-power passive tap (like the Throwing Star LAN Tap already in this database) never does. Where it genuinely wins is standalone capture: no laptop needed, just plug in a USB drive and walk away, and it explicitly passes 802.1X traffic through untouched rather than trying to defeat it.

build_note: Sold pre-assembled and tested with a Micro USB cable included; open-source firmware is user-reflashable via Arduino IDE.
summary: The base model in the Netgotchi line: an ESP8266 + small OLED board that periodically scans the local 2.4GHz Wi-Fi network for hosts and runs a honeypot service, sounding an on-screen alarm (the on-screen character 'crying') if the honeypot is touched. Same firmware as Netgotchi Pro, in a smaller/cheaper non-portable form.
honest_take: Identical function to the pricier Netgotchi Pro - same open-source code (MXZZ/Netgotchi), same ESP8266 scan-and-honeypot behavior, same 2.4GHz-only limitation, same complete blindness to actual attacker RF hardware (Pineapples, Flippers, rogue APs) since it only watches hosts on the one network it joins. At $15 less than the Pro, this is the better buy for anyone who doesn't specifically need the Pro's pocket-portable case, since the detection capability is the same either way.
best_for: Cheapest way into this exact firmware/detection behavior
A fixed desk/shelf placement rather than portable use
not_for: Detecting Wi-Fi/BLE attacker hardware - it only scans hosts on its own joined network
Portable/pocket use (see Netgotchi Pro for that)

hardware.battery_note: No internal battery; USB powered from an external power bank or wall adapter (not included).
hardware.charging: USB (from external power bank or wall adapter, not included)

wifi_scan_24.note: Periodic ping-sweep of the local 2.4GHz network to report new/active hosts.

standalone_untethered.note: Runs its scan/honeypot loop independently once configured, needs only USB power.

web_ui.note: Initial Wi-Fi credential setup via an AutoConnectAP captive portal.

usb_hid_inject.note: Not a USB-HID device; it's a network scanner/honeypot.

ble_scan.note: ESP8266 has no Bluetooth hardware at all, unlike ESP32-based devices.

app_store.note: No companion mobile app; configuration is via its own captive-portal web page.

cloud_c2.note: No cloud dependency; operates entirely on the local network it joins.

ethernet_tap_passive.note: Wi-Fi only device, no wired network interface.

legal.notes: Purely defensive; legal to build, own, and run on a network you control.
